problems.title: Charts for comparison and trend questions
problems.prompt:
Using temperature data from one summer day, draw two charts side by side that answer two questions. The left chart (`ax1`) compares five cities to show which was hottest, and the right chart (`ax2`) shows how the temperature in Seoul changed over that day.
In each of the two blanks, write the drawing command that fits the question. Draw a bar chart with `bar(x values, bar heights)` and a line chart with `plot(x values, y values)`.
hints: A bar chart fits a comparison question, which asks which one is bigger. A line chart fits a trend question, which asks how something changes over time.
The bar heights are `high`, and the y values of the line are `seoul`. Pair them with `cities` and `hours`, respectively, which go on the x-axis.
problems.explain:
The left question compares the temperatures of five cities, so it is a comparison question, and `ax1.bar(cities, high)` draws a bar for each city. The right question asks about change over the day, so it is a trend question, and `ax2.plot(hours, seoul)` connects the temperature at each time with a line. Even with temperature data from the same day, a different question calls for a different chart.
If you swap the two commands, the charts draw without errors, but the line connects cities that have no natural order, so it looks as if something flows from one city to the next. If you leave out the x values, as in `plot(seoul)`, the x-axis shows position numbers starting at 0 instead of the times. Grading checks the chart types along with the bar heights and the line values, and redraws the charts with different temperatures.

problems.title: Charts for distribution and relationship questions

problems.explain:
How the steps are spread out is a distribution question. `ax1.hist(steps)` divides the range of steps into bins and draws the number of days in each bin as the bar height. If you connect the points with a line, as in `plot(temp, power)`, they are joined in the order they were recorded, so the line zigzags back and forth. If you swap the two values, the temperature goes on the y-axis and no longer matches the axis labels. This problem does not set the number of bins, so the histogram uses the default of 10 bins.

problems.prompt:
You asked an AI to draw a bar chart of a bakery's sales by item, and it gave you this draft. The y-axis starts at 40, so the differences between the bars look bigger than they really are, and the title adds a judgment that is not in the data.
Fix two lines so that the y-axis shows 0 to 60 and the title becomes `Bakery sales by item, Oct 14`, which states what was measured and when.
hints: A bar shows its value by its length from the bottom to the top. If the bottom of the axis is cut off, the ratio of the lengths no longer matches the ratio of the values, so look for the line that sets the range.

problems.title: Figure and Axes under swapped names
problems.prompt:
This code deliberately unpacks the two values returned by `plt.subplots()` in the order `ax, fig`. Write what it prints when it runs.
`type(value).__name__` returns only the name of the value's type (class). A Figure's `axes` attribute returns the Axes in that Figure as a list.
hints: `plt.subplots()` returns the Figure first and the Axes second. The names of the variables that receive them do not change this order.
Trace what is actually stored in the variable named `fig`. Then check which way that object's `xaxis` runs.
problems.explain:
`plt.subplots()` always returns two values in the order Figure, Axes. So the name `ax` holds the Figure, and the name `fig` holds the Axes. `fig.xaxis` is the x-axis of that Axes, so its type is XAxis, and `ax.axes` is the list of Axes in the Figure, so its length is 1.
The names `fig` and `ax` are a convention that helps people read the code. Python does not decide a value's type from the variable name. Reversed names confuse readers, so in real code keep the order `fig, ax`.

print(type(fig.xaxis).__name__)

problems.title: Splitting the work between the Figure and the Axes
problems.prompt: Draw a line chart of the campus radio station's listeners by time slot and save it to a file. In the five blanks, write the name of the object that receives each command. Commands that change the whole figure go to `fig`, and commands that change the one chart area where the line is drawn go to `ax`.
hints: Look at how far the job in each comment reaches. The line and the chart title above it sit inside the Axes, while the figure title at the very top, the margins, and the saved file cover the whole figure.

`fig` is the Figure, the first value returned by `plt.subplots()`, and `ax` is the Axes, the second value. `suptitle()`, which adds the figure title, and `savefig()`, which saves the figure to a file, are Figure methods.
problems.explain:
`fig` is the Figure, which refers to the whole figure, and `ax` is the Axes on it where the line is drawn. Drawing the line and the chart title stay inside the Axes, so they are done with `ax.plot()` and `ax.set_title()`. The figure title at the top, tidying the margins, and saving the file affect the whole figure, so they are done with `fig.suptitle()`, `fig.tight_layout()`, and `fig.savefig()`.
If you pick the wrong object, you call a method that the object does not have, and you get an AttributeError. `ax.savefig()` and `fig.plot()` are examples. A job for the whole figure can also be called through `plt`, as in `plt.suptitle()`. It applies to the current figure, so you get the same figure.

require.message: The figure title, tidying the margins, and saving the file affect the whole figure, so the Figure (`fig`) receives them. Using `plt` gives the same figure, but this problem is practice in splitting the work between the Figure and the Axes.

problems.title: The current Axes that plt commands act on
problems.prompt: This code draws listener charts for the campus radio station's morning show and night show in the `plt` style. Trace which Figure's Axes each command applies to, and write what the code prints when it runs. You can get the Axes in a Figure as a list with `fig.axes`.
hints: Each call to `plt.figure()` creates a new empty figure with no Axes, and the `plt` commands after it target that figure.
Like `plt.plot()`, `plt.title()` goes on an Axes of the current figure. If the current figure has no Axes, it first creates a new empty Axes and puts the title on it.
problems.explain:
The `fig` made by `plt.figure()` has no Axes yet, so 0 is printed. The next `plt.plot()` creates one Axes in `fig` and draws the line, and `plt.title()` puts a title on that Axes, so `fig` now has 1 Axes.
When `fig2 = plt.figure()` runs, the current figure switches to `fig2`. So the next `plt.title()` creates a new empty Axes in `fig2` and puts the title on it, and each figure has 1 Axes. In the `plt` style, the order of the lines decides which figure receives a command, so if one `plt.figure()` line slips in between, every command after it goes to the new figure. If you put the Axes in front of each command, as in `ax.set_title()`, each line shows its target, so this confusion does not happen.
problems.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
print(len(fig.axes))
plt.plot(["6am", "7am", "8am"], [35, 58, 47])
plt.title("Morning show listeners")
print(len(fig.axes))
fig2 = plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
plt.title("Night show listeners")
print(len(fig.axes), len(fig2.axes))
problems.solution:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

problems.title: Vending machine sales outside the 1.5×IQR bounds
problems.prompt:
The list `cans` holds the number of drinks (cans) that each of ten campus vending machines sold in a day. Find Q1 and Q3 with pandas `quantile()`, and use the IQR (`Q3 - Q1`) to compute the lower bound `Q1 - 1.5 * IQR` and the upper bound `Q3 + 1.5 * IQR`.
Pick the values below the lower bound or above the upper bound as possible outliers, and print them once with `print()` as a Python list sorted from smallest to largest. If the same value is a possible outlier more than once, include it that many times. With the given values, the code prints `[25]`, and if there are no possible outliers, it prints `[]`. Print nothing else. Grading runs the code again with different values in `cans`.
hints: `s.quantile(0.25)` and `s.quantile(0.75)` are Q1 and Q3. pandas computes them by linear interpolation between values.
A value equal to a bound is not a possible outlier. If you pick values as a pandas Series or a NumPy array, turn them into a Python list with `.tolist()` before you print.
problems.explain:
With the given values, Q1 is 8 and Q3 is 9.75, so the IQR is 1.75. The bounds are 8 - 2.625 = 5.375 and 9.75 + 2.625 = 12.375, and the only value outside them is 25. The bounds are calculated values that separate possible outliers, and the whiskers of a box plot are drawn to the outermost observations inside them, 7 and 11. The vending machine that sold 25 cans is a possible outlier whose sales record should be checked again.
A value equal to a bound is inside the bounds, so select with `<` and `>`. For `[10, 12, 14, 16, 22]`, the upper bound is 22, so 22 is not a possible outlier. Each possible outlier is a record to check, so if the same value appears twice, include both. If you reduce repeated values to one with `set()` or `unique()`, records to check go missing.

import pandas as pd

cans = [8, 9, 7, 10, 9, 8, 25, 9, 11, 8]

# Write your code here
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

cans = [8, 9, 7, 10, 9, 8, 25, 9, 11, 8]

s = pd.Series(cans)
q1 = s.quantile(0.25)
q3 = s.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
lower = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
outliers = sorted(v for v in cans if v < lower or v > upper)
print(outliers)

On the bottom Axes, plot one dot per student. Put the part-time hours on the x-axis and the group names (`Dorm`, `Home`) on the y-axis, and plot `dorm` first. To keep the dots from being jittered (shifted slightly at random), pass `jitter=False` to seaborn's `stripplot()`, or plot them with Matplotlib's `scatter()`. The title is `One dot per student`, and only the top Axes has a legend.

hints: Call `kdeplot()` once for each group and give it `label` and `linestyle`. Show the legend only on the top Axes with `axes[0].legend()`.

problems.explain:
The density curves on the top Axes show the shapes of the two groups, and the dots on the bottom Axes show the value of each student. Because the two Axes share the x-axis, you can line them up from top to bottom and see whether the dots bunch up where a curve is high. Dorm students cluster at 6 to 12 hours a week, so their curve is narrow and tall, while students who commute from home spread widely from 3 to 19 hours. `cut=0` stops each curve within the range of the observations, so it is not drawn into negative part-time hours.
The smooth shape of a density curve changes with the settings and the sample size, so read small samples like 10 and 8 students together with the raw data points. The height of a curve does not tell you the number of observations, so put it in the figure title with `len()`. By default, `stripplot()` jitters the dots, shifting each one slightly at random. This problem grades the positions of the dots, so it uses `jitter=False`; then equal values, such as 7, 8, and 9 hours, overlap as one dot. If you draw both curves at once with `hue`, it is hard to set a line style for each group, and the default `common_norm=True` scales the heights by looking at both groups together, so the curve of the group with fewer students comes out lower.
